To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the antenna geometry and the SiO2 layer thickness are critical for the performance of the antenna-coupled thermoelectric devices, and that all-Ni antenna is the best choice for the antenna material.
the all-Au antenna has the best thermal response, the Au/Ni/Au antenna has the worst thermal response, and the Ni/Au/Ni antenna has a thermal response between these two extremes.

the Au-Ni-Au antenna with a Ni center segment dissipates more power in the antenna and has a larger temperature rise at the center than the all-Au and all-Ni antennas; that the SiO2 layer thickness should be 0.5 microns or more to reduce heat dissipation into the Si substrate; and that the mesh size of the antenna and Si substrate must be less than 0.1 microns to avoid mesh-related simulation errors.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of antennas that can convert THz radiation into heat efficiently, and the design of nanothermocoupes that can convert this heat into electrical signals with minimal loss.
the development of a nanothermocoupling system that can be used to measure temperature in the THz range.
the development of antenna-coupled thermoelectric detectors for the terahertz (THz) spectral range.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the all-Ni antenna with 1 μm of thermal insulation is the best choice, and that this is the antenna design we will use for our experiments.

the Au-Ni-Au antennas with 10 nm Ni center segment, 20 nm SiO2 insulation, and 20 nm Au-Ni-Ausubstrate are the best choice in terms of antenna efficiency, heat transfer to the substrate, heat transfer to nanothermocoule, and heat transfer to the environment.

the Au/Ni/Au antenna has a better heat distribution than all-Au or all-Ni antenna, and the SiO2 layer should be at least 1.5 micrometers thick to minimize thermal losses into the Si substrate.
